item.title: When a Tree Got a Seat Number
item.summary: A school learns to label seedlings by the decisions people need to make later.
item.content_markdown:
After a heavy delivery, the school grounds team found that several young trees now had labels reading only “new tree”. The old labels had been cut off with the wrapping. The trees had been supplied as two different batches, and the planting plan treated the groups differently. One group would go along the open path and the other against a brick wall. A photograph of the delivery van would not tell the team which tree had come out of which wrapping.

The nursery sent two batch photographs showing bands of different colours around the stems. Those bands were still on the trees. The groundskeeper used them to tell the batches apart and then marked each pot with a number. In her first list, each number identified a tree. The pupils helping her said the numbers looked like places in an audience, especially once the pots were lined up by the gate. They used the pot numbers to find trees in that first row and carried each tree to the place they had been given.

Later, during the first term, the school replaced one tree beside the wall. A committee member asked whether the replacement needed the care given to the tree that used to be there. On the list, number sixteen still referred to the tree that had been taken away. It would have been easy to write over the row with a new note. That would remove the record of what had happened to the first tree, just when the school wanted to understand how well the space worked.

The groundskeeper kept the original number with each tree and gave each planting position its own letter. A, B and C were fixed places on the plan, and trees could come and go there. Now the pupils can ask about a tree's history or about every tree that has occupied a position by the wall. Nobody has yet collected a long record for every spot. The new labels make such a record possible. The school had started by listing what it owned. It ended up needing a way to follow what changed in the grounds.
item.theme: keeping plant records attached to planting sites

questions.prompt: What does this article mainly distinguish?
options: The names of trees bought in different seasons
A tree's identity and the place where it happens to stand
The plots the school planted and those a builder will use
The branches that are healthy and those that need cutting
questions.explanation: The second labels give each fixed site a separate identifier from the tree, allowing either history to be followed.

questions.prompt: What made the original batch labels unavailable?
options: The groundskeeper used them as markers on the wall.
A group of pupils returned them to the driver.
They had been removed along with the packaging.
Rain destroyed every label at the same time.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says the old labels had been cut off with the wrapping.

questions.prompt: Why did the groundskeeper keep the entry for the removed tree?
options: The next pupil might find the same tree inside the delivery van.
The school wanted to plant it in position sixteen again.
The replacement had already been included in the first delivery photo.
The record might help people understand the history of the spot.
questions.explanation: A new entry about the replacement should not erase what previously occupied the place.

questions.prompt: What does “write over the row” mean here?
options: Replace the information already on the record
Move the row of pots nearer the wall
Add another group of labelled trees at the gate
Draw a new path over the planting positions
questions.explanation: The sentence contrasts putting new information into a row with preserving what it already records.

questions.prompt: The first numbers referred to individual trees.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph explicitly explains what a number identified.

questions.prompt: The same number now follows a position rather than a tree.
questions.explanation: Numbers stay with the trees; fixed positions have their own letters.

questions.prompt: The article says why the tree beside the wall was replaced.
questions.explanation: It reports a replacement, but no cause for removing the earlier tree is given.

questions.prompt: Complete the sentences with words from the passage.
questions.text: The first pots stood in a row near the ___. Each planting position finally gets a ___.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 names the gate and paragraph 4 gives letters to the fixed positions.

questions.prompt: Choose the best heading for each numbered paragraph.
options: An omission becomes important when a tree is replaced
A delivery with missing labels
Two references for two histories
Making a list of the individual trees
Changing where the wall is built
questions.explanation: The article starts with lost batch details, introduces individual numbers, then tests them against a replacement before distinguishing tree and position records.
